title: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
desc: Extends responsibility to leaders and supervisors while preserving proportionate checking rather than duplicating every automated step.

kps.k: AI assistance does not transfer professional responsibility: lawyers must retain judgment, and judges must retain judicial authority.
kps.d: The cluster frames responsible AI use as an application of existing competence, candour, confidentiality and supervision duties, not an exemption from them. ABA Opinion 512 permits AI-generated drafts and analyses as starting points but rejects sole reliance for functions requiring professional judgment. Ayinde extends responsibility to lawyers relying on others’ AI-assisted work; Lnu v. Blanche applies the same checking duties even when lawyers neither use nor suspect AI. These propositions support augmentation rather than autonomous substitution. Their legal force remains jurisdiction-specific: ABA Model Rules, state rules, judicial orders and advisory professional guidance are not interchangeable.

qs.q: While GAI may be used as a springboard or foundation for legal work—for example, by generating an analysis on which a lawyer bases legal advice, or by generating a draft from which a lawyer produces a legal document—lawyers may not abdicate their responsibilities by relying solely on a GAI tool to perform tasks that call for the exercise of professional judgment.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 512: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: This duty rests on lawyers who use artificial intelligence to conduct research themselves            or rely on the work of others who have done so.
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Verification means checking substantive support, not merely detecting nonexistent citations.
kps.d: Courts and professional bodies require lawyers to establish that authorities exist, quotations are accurate, propositions follow from the sources, and work fits the facts, jurisdiction and client’s interests. Ayinde identifies authoritative external sources as the critical safeguard and rejects a tribunal’s suggestion that asking the model to abstain or identify weaknesses materially reduces risk. Texas Opinion 705 and Lnu stress that removing fabrications does not discharge the duty to reason independently. The practical implication is source-level review and substantive legal analysis before reliance, rather than accepting a chatbot’s assurance or treating automated citation checking as sufficient.

qs.q: Those who use artificial intelligence to conduct legal research notwithstanding these            risks have a professional duty therefore to check the accuracy of such research by            reference to authoritative sources, before using it in the course of their professional            work (to advise clients or before a court, for example).
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: That said, a lawyer’s duties require more than merely detecting and eliminating false AI-generated results—the lawyer is ultimately responsible for ensuring that the content is accurate and supports the client’s interests.
qs.a: Texas Professional Ethics Committee Opinion 705: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The extent of verification remains task-sensitive; rigorous filing checks do not necessarily require duplicating every automated task.
kps.d: ABA Opinion 512 allows testing contract summaries against a manually reviewed subset rather than necessarily rereading an entire collection, and recognises that prior experience with discrete-task tools may justify less review. Singapore’s sector guide similarly scales oversight to task risk and calls for greater scrutiny outside the practitioner’s expertise. CCBE qualifies verification by use case, including risk-free tasks and comprehensively informed recipients of unverified output. These approaches differ in scope from categorical checking requirements for court authorities. None establishes a general exemption from professional judgment or overrides applicable filing rules.

qs.q: Moreover, a lawyer’s use of a GAI tool designed specifically for the practice of law or to perform a discrete legal task, such as generating ideas, may require less independent verification or review, particularly where a lawyer’s prior experience with the GAI tool provides a reasonable basis for relying on its results.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 512: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: When using GenAI tools in areas          outside their subject matter expertise, legal professionals should exercise greater          scrutiny to identify potential hallucinations and biases, and take additional steps to          verify output against authoritative sources and reference materials.17       (e) Mitigate potential biases.
qs.a: Guide for Using Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Sector · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Specialised tools may improve research, but product labels and repeated sanctions stories do not establish reliability.
kps.d: ABA Opinion 512 and the Bar Council cite Stanford’s 2024 legal-research study as reporting hallucinations on 17–33% of queries in tested specialised systems. Oregon separately reports Stanford research on general-purpose models answering questions about courts’ core rulings; its reported figure of at least 75% concerns a different task and model category. Neither figure is a universal or current error rate. The Hallucination-Free? authors call for product-specific empirical evidence while acknowledging that imperfect tools can help initiate research. Limited access to bespoke systems further constrains comparisons. Court incidents establish concrete failures and consequences, not their prevalence.

qs.q: For example, in a test      examining more than 200,000 legal questions, AI researchers at Stanford University found      that general-purpose large language models—including Meta, Google, and OpenAI      programs—hallucinate at least 75% of the time when answering questions about a court’s      core rulings.
qs.a: Oregon State Bar Formal Opinion No. 2025-205: Artificial Intelligence · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: In other words, lawyers’ ability to comply with their professional duties in both of these jurisdictions is contingent on access to specific information about empirical risks and benefits of legal AI.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Accountability increasingly reaches supervisors and institutional leaders, not just the person entering prompts.
kps.d: Ayinde concludes that publishing guidance alone has not secured compliance and calls for effective measures by managing partners, heads of chambers and regulators, with future scrutiny of leadership responsibilities. Cassata connects effective supervision to understanding the AI-enhanced research tool an associate uses. Canadian and California guidance recommends approved-use policies, staff training, audits and continuing reassessment. California expressly treats greater agentic autonomy as a reason for stronger controls and prohibits autonomous filings or court communications. Policies therefore need operational enforcement; their existence does not itself discharge individual duties.

qs.q: These Hamid cases show that promulgating such guidance on its own is         insufficient to address the misuse of artificial intelligence.
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: The Court finds incompatable the concept that a supervising attorney can properly supervise an associate regarding the proper use of technology provided by the law firm (Artificial Intelligence version of Westlaw), with the concept herein conceded that the supervising attorney does not know how to use it.
qs.a: Cassata v. Michael Macrina Architect, P.C. — AI sanctions decision, Suffolk County · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Sanctions protect clients and court processes, but culpability, mitigation and proof of AI involvement still matter.
kps.d: The sources report costs orders, disciplinary referrals, practice restrictions and other sanctions for unchecked material. Their rationale extends beyond lawyer reputation: fabricated authorities consume opponents’ and courts’ resources and can displace sound arguments. Negligence can carry consequences without deliberate deception, but contempt and criminal escalation require separate analysis. Ayinde declines to initiate contempt proceedings against Mr Hussain while retaining regulatory referral. Ko v. Li expressly leaves AI involvement unproven at the show-cause stage. Suspicious citations, denied AI use and confirmed AI fabrication must therefore remain distinct.

qs.q: While one party can create a fake legal brief          at the click of a button, the opposing party and court must parse through the case          names, citations, and points of law to determine which parts, if any, are true.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

qs.q: The         threshold for the initiation of contempt proceedings is, accordingly, not met.
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The main regulatory disagreement concerns additional safeguards, not whether humans remain responsible.
kps.d: Browning favours education and supervision over AI-specific regulation, questioning whether mandatory disclosures and certificates add value beyond Rule 11. New York Formal Opinion 2024-5 likewise favours adaptable guardrails over rigid restrictions. By contrast, The Promise and the Peril treats education, certification, sanctions and prohibition as complementary, revisable responses. Actual court requirements vary: New Zealand generally requires disclosure only when asked, England and Wales makes it context-dependent, and judge-specific US orders impose certification or disclosure. Practitioners must distinguish these operative local requirements from proposals, commentary and professional recommendations.

qs.q: Like the California State Bar and other bar associations that have addressed Generative AI,2 we believe that when addressing developing areas, lawyers need guardrails and not hard-and-fast restrictions or new rules that could stymie developments.
qs.a: Formal Opinion 2024-5 — Ethical Obligations of Lawyers and Law Firms Relating to the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Each of the solutions has a role to play and they are generally mutually reinforcing.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Confidentiality requires tool-specific data controls; consent and enterprise branding are not complete safeguards.
kps.d: Guidance identifies risks from provider access, retention, training reuse, cross-client retrieval and security breaches. Judicial guidance in England and Wales prohibits non-public inputs into public chatbots; NSW permits specified protected litigation material only under controlled-environment, confidentiality and no-training conditions. Other professional guidance allows context-dependent consent or exceptions where disclosure occurs. The Canadian toolkit stresses that consent cannot prevent harm or excuse professional breaches. Procurement and supervision should therefore examine actual data practices, access controls, ethical screens and incident procedures, including clients’ own use of transcription or drafting tools.

qs.q: Uphold confidentiality and privacy  Do not enter any information into a public AI chatbot that is not already in the public domain.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Many legal instruments and policies now recognize that AI systems are not sufficiently comprehensible to allow for meaningful consent relating to its use and that harm may be caused and professional obligations breached, even with consent.
qs.a: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence for the Legal Practitioner · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Judicial decision-making and witness evidence attract safeguards beyond ordinary drafting review.
kps.d: Canadian Judicial Council and Hong Kong guidance prohibit delegation of judicial authority; England and Wales requires judges to read underlying documents and engage directly with evidence. Vos supports checked drafting and research but leaves AI’s proper decision-making role as a difficult societal question. Evidence rules also differ: Singapore allows compliant first-cut affidavit drafts while prohibiting fabrication or tampering; NSW prohibits generating or rephrasing witness evidence, preserves preparatory work, and requires prior leave for expert-report generation subject to stated exceptions. These distinctions prevent general permission for drafting from becoming permission to manufacture evidence or outsource adjudication.

qs.q: It must be unequivocally understood that no judge is permitted to delegate decision-making authority, whether to a law clerk, administrative assistant, or computer program, regardless of their capabilities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: AI tools may assist, but they cannot replace direct judicial engagement with evidence.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Verification costs and retained expertise qualify claims of efficiency and access to justice.
kps.d: D.C. Opinion 388 warns that checking costs may outweigh anticipated benefits; Australian regulators caution against unnecessarily increasing client costs through verification and correction. California limits hourly billing to actual time rather than time saved. For self-represented litigants, judicial guidance and litigation scholarship identify a different constraint: awareness of errors may not supply the legal expertise or research access needed to check them. AI may be some litigants’ only assistance, yet unchecked output can damage their case and shift costs to others. These sources present accessibility and productivity gains as conditional, not established by cheap generation alone.

qs.q: At some point, however, the time and costs associated with the verification may outweigh whatever perceived benefits led the lawyer to consider using the GAI in the first place.
qs.a: D.C. Bar Ethics Opinion 388: Attorneys' Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Client Matters · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Generative AI Costs   Hourly billing must reflect the time actually spent on the client’s                       matter, recognizing that generative AI may reduce the time required Rule 1.5                       for certain tasks.
qs.a: Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Preserving the expertise needed to supervise AI creates a further dispute over education and adoption.
kps.d: CCBE and Singapore recommend retaining core legal-task training alongside AI literacy. Artificial Intelligence and Human Legal Reasoning warns that faster answers may weaken internalised understanding and proposes asking whether lawyers can independently defend their work. Its reported deterioration after AI revision occurred under fatigue and a twenty-minute revision limit, so it does not establish universal skill loss. Closing the AI Readiness Gap advocates informed selective use; The Verification-Value Paradox recommends restricting assessment use and discouraging AI-assisted learning. Texas Opinion 705 almost certainly rejects a current adoption duty, while The Legal Ethics of Generative AI predicts one may eventually arise. These are competing educational prescriptions and conditional forecasts.

qs.q: Therefore, it is        essential that the training of lawyers in the performance of the underlying tasks should not        be neglected.
qs.a: CCBE Guide on the Use of Generative AI by Lawyers · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: A useful heuristic is to ask, before relying on AI-generated work product, whether the lawyer could defend that work product in a demanding conversation with a skeptical colleague or judge without further preparation.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and Human Legal Reasoning · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The curated academia and research sources generally accept the proposition’s core: AI assistance does not displace lawyers’ professional judgment or accountability, and verification must establish that authorities exist, are accurate and relevant, and actually support the propositions asserted. They commonly ground this view in existing duties of competence, candour, confidentiality and supervision; reported hallucination incidents and sanctions illustrate the consequences of failure but are not treated as measures of prevalence. Collectively, the sources materially develop the proposition in several ways. They identify automation bias, verification drift, legal-literacy gaps and time pressure as mechanisms that can undermine checking; propose an independent-defensibility test for retained professional understanding; and argue that responsible deployment requires empirical, product-specific evaluation to identify suitable tasks and calibrate oversight. They also show why verification can qualify claimed efficiency and access-to-justice gains, particularly where unrepresented litigants lack the expertise or research access needed to check outputs. Material internal variation concerns safeguards rather than human responsibility: some favour education and supervision over additional AI-specific regulation, while others treat certification, sanctions and revisable prohibitions as complementary; educational prescriptions range from informed selective use to restricting AI-assisted learning and assessment; and one source predicts that competence may eventually require AI use while others reject any current adoption duty. Several fragmentary or reliability-focused excerpts do not themselves establish a position on supervisory accountability, so this synthesis should not be read as representing academia generally or as evidence of prevalence within that professional voice.

qs.q: Under Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, legal contentions must be warranted by existing law or supported by a nonfrivolous argument for changing it, which means attorneys must verify that the legal authorities on which they rely actually exist and support the propositions for which they are cited.
qs.a: Closing the AI Readiness Gap: A Framework for Law Schools · Academia · 2026

qs.q: In other words, lawyers’ ability to comply with their professional duties in both of these jurisdictions is contingent on access to specific information about empirical risks and benefits of legal AI.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: Within this curated professional voice, the sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition that AI assistance leaves lawyers responsible for judgment, supervision and verification. Their common reasoning is risk-based: unchecked output may introduce inaccurate material into client work or court filings, while AI-generated records can also threaten confidentiality and privilege. They materially extend the proposition by applying accountability beyond a lawyer’s own prompting to subordinates’ work and clients’ use of GenAI, including client-edited documents and AI recordings or transcripts. Internal variation concerns scope and specificity: the reported Nigerian Bar Association guidance states a broad duty of critical review and responsible supervision but does not articulate the cluster’s fuller source-level test of whether authorities substantively support propositions or how review should be proportioned by task. The loss-prevention source is more operational and filing-focused, requiring thorough verification and concrete controls where clients use GenAI. Its references to sanctions and other consequences are framed as risks rather than documented outcomes in the excerpt.

qs.q: Critically review outputs generated by AI tools before relying on them in client work.
qs.a: Nigerian Bar Association Launches New Technology Guidelines for Legal Practice · Market & press · 2024

qs.q: If a lawyer fails to thoroughly verify the accuracy of these outputs and files documents containing hallucinations, the lawyer may face judicial reprimand, sanction, and other professional discipline.
qs.a: Loss Prevention Takeaways — You, Me, and ChatGPT: How firms can educate clients about the dangers of uploading privileged or confidential information into GenAI platforms · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The legal-tech vendor source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI assistance does not transfer professional responsibility and that human verification must precede reliance. It grounds accountability in existing professional and procedural duties, especially attorneys’ personal responsibility for filings, and endorses independent review against primary legal authorities rather than treating AI as authoritative. It also extends caution beyond lawyers to judges and self-represented litigants. The main qualification is that it frames review categorically—stating that all AI-generated content requires verification—without developing the cluster’s task-sensitive, proportionate approach or its emphasis on supervisory and institutional accountability. It additionally claims that legal-specific platforms are substantially safer than consumer tools without supplying comparative measurements; this sits somewhat uneasily with the cluster’s warning that product labels and features do not themselves establish reliability. These are limitations rather than rejection of the core proposition. As the evidence comprises one curated vendor source, it does not establish the position of legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 and its state counterparts establish clear certification requirements for court filings, making attorneys personally responsible for verifying all submitted content, regardless of its technological origin.
qs.a: From 'trust but verify' to 'do not trust until verified': How the legal profession is redefining AI accountability · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The professional-liability insurer source supports the proposition’s core claim that AI use does not displace human and institutional responsibility. Its distinctive rationale is risk and liability management: inaccurate or unfair outputs can create additional exposure, particularly where firms lack human review, staff training, risk assessment, and enforceable internal controls. It therefore reinforces the proposition’s extension of accountability beyond individual users to firm-level governance. The source also recognises broad legal uses and predicts expanding adoption, but this is not opposition; it treats opportunity and control as compatible. Materially, however, it is less specific than the cluster proposition: it calls for monitoring and checking outputs but does not establish that verification must examine authoritative sources, confirm that authorities support the stated propositions, or be calibrated proportionately by task. Because the evidence represents one curated insurer source, it supports a liability-focused perspective rather than establishing the position of professional-liability insurers generally.

qs.q: -  Have appropriate internal policies and frameworks in place to govern use of AI tools, to monitor the AI’s outputs and to rectify issues with the AI models.
qs.a: Law firm AI: insurance considerations · Liability insurers · 2024

vlens.an:
The curated regulators, courts and professional-body sources strongly support the proposition. Their common rationale is that AI is an assistive tool rather than a bearer of professional or judicial duties: lawyers remain responsible for competence, candour, confidentiality and the substantive quality of work, while judges retain decision-making authority. Verification therefore commonly extends beyond detecting fabricated citations to checking authoritative sources, factual and legal accuracy, jurisdictional applicability, completeness, relevance and whether authorities actually support the propositions asserted. Many sources also place operational duties on supervisors and institutional leaders through approved-use policies, technological competence, staff training, audits, vendor and data controls, and continuing reassessment.

Material variation concerns safeguards rather than the underlying allocation of responsibility. Some guidance requires categorical, source-level checks for court filings and authorities; other guidance expressly makes verification proportionate to the tool, task, prior testing and risk, allowing sampling or lighter review for discrete, lower-risk uses. Disclosure also varies from generally unnecessary or context-dependent to mandatory under particular court orders or recommended where provenance, client expectations or contestability matter. Judicial decision-making, witness evidence, expert reports, protected information and agentic court communications attract stricter limits than routine drafting, summaries or administrative work. Some sources favour adaptable existing-duty guardrails, whereas others add certifications, disclosure, contestability or lifecycle governance. Courts provide concrete findings about misconduct and sanctions, while much professional guidance is prescriptive and its risk claims or cited performance figures should not be treated as universal empirical rates. The sources also preserve distinctions between proven AI fabrication, suspicious authorities where AI involvement is unproven, and ordinary lawyer error.

qs.q: Therefore, it is essential that barristers (and all legal practitioners) verify that any sources or authorities cited by such systems actually support the propositions asserted, and ensure that the citations are accurate and extant.
qs.a: Considerations when using ChatGPT and generative artificial intelligence software based on large language models (November 2025 update) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: In those circumstances, practical and effective measures must now be taken by those            within the legal profession with individual leadership responsibilities (such as heads of            chambers and managing partners) and by those with the responsibility for regulating            the provision of legal services.
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The 2015–2022 sources support the proposition’s core claim that AI assistance does not transfer professional responsibility: lawyers must retain independent professional judgment and should not adopt AI-generated analysis without checking it. Their common reasoning is ethical and precautionary rather than empirical. Both connect responsible reliance to understanding or testing the tool’s effectiveness, while the ROSS-focused source specifically warns that polished work product and time pressure can induce failures to verify accuracy. There is some internal variation: the effectiveness-focused source takes a conditional, permissive approach, suggesting that consistently demonstrated reliability could reduce the need for client approval or consent; the ROSS-focused source more strongly condemns sole or blind reliance as potentially violating Model Rule 2.1. These sources nevertheless address a narrower proposition than the completed synthesis. They focus principally on the individual lawyer, accuracy checking, client communication and independent judgment; they do not materially develop the later synthesis’s requirements for source-level substantive support, task-sensitive verification, supervisory and institutional accountability, judicial authority, or sanctions. Because the corpus is curated, this alignment characterises these supplied sources rather than the period or legal profession generally.

qs.q: If effectiveness testing consistently shows             reliance on AI could raise questions about whether that an AI tool is reliable and does not present risks              the lawyer’s “professional judgment” remains “inde- and limitations, arguably neither client approval nor               pendent.” For example, this issue could arise if a law- informed consent should be required.
qs.a: Evaluating Artificial Intelligence for Legal Services: Can ‘Soft Law’ Lead to Enforceable Standards for Effectiveness? · Academia · 2021

qs.q: 121      In terms of implementing the work of an AI lawyer to a case, when a lawyer relies solely on ROSS’s outputs, independent professional judgment—as required by Model Rule 2.1—vanishes because reliance on such outputs turns into dependence on the judgments of a technological apparatus.
qs.a: Artificially Intelligent Lawyers: Updating the Model Rules of Professional Conduct in Accordance with the New Technological Era · Academia · 2018

elens.an:
The curated 2023–2024 sources strongly support the cluster’s principal proposition. In response to the generative-AI shock—especially plausible but fabricated authorities and resulting sanctions—professional bodies, courts, regulators and commentators generally treated AI as assistive rather than a substitute for accountable legal or judicial judgment. Their common reasoning is that fluent output can conceal factual, legal, jurisdictional and citation errors; therefore existing duties of competence, candour, confidentiality and supervision continue to attach to the human user. Several sources expressly go beyond checking whether citations exist: they require review of accuracy, sufficiency, relevance, reliability, evidentiary support, legal warrant, applicability to the facts and jurisdiction, and alignment with client interests. The period also operationalises supervisory accountability through approved-tool policies, staff training, active oversight, audits, data controls and responsibility for AI-assisted work produced by subordinates or support staff.

Material variation concerns implementation rather than the core principle. ABA Opinion 512 and some Australian and international guidance favour task- and risk-sensitive verification, including validated sampling or lighter review for discrete, previously tested tools; filing authorities and higher-risk legal work attract more rigorous checking. D.C. guidance and Australian regulators also caution that verification costs can erase efficiency gains or increase client costs. Disclosure rules differ: some judge-specific orders require disclosure or certification, New Zealand generally does not require routine disclosure unless asked, and other guidance makes disclosure dependent on confidentiality, novelty, provenance or client circumstances. Browning and New York Formal Opinion 2024-5 prefer education and adaptable guardrails over additional rigid regulation, whereas some courts impose AI-specific safeguards. Judicial sources add a categorical non-delegation rule for adjudication, and evidence-related guidance distinguishes permissible drafting assistance from fabricating or manipulating evidence. Sources addressing self-represented litigants recognise that AI may be their only assistance while also questioning their capacity to verify it.

The evidentiary basis should be kept in perspective: much of this material is normative or advisory guidance, supported by reported sanctions incidents and prospective risk claims rather than original measurements of effectiveness or prevalence. Predictions about wider adoption, efficiency, access to justice and an eventual duty to use AI remain conditional. The sources are a curated selection, so their convergence cannot be treated as evidence that every institution or practitioner in the period held the same view.

The curated 2025 sources strongly support the proposition that scaling legal AI does not transfer professional or judicial responsibility and that verification must examine substantive legal support. Across court judgments, practice notes, ethics opinions and professional guidance, the recurring rationale is that fluent output may contain fabricated, inaccurate, outdated, biased or jurisdictionally inapplicable material; accordingly, users must check authorities and conclusions against reliable or authoritative sources, retain independent judgment, and remain accountable for submitted work. Several sources also reinforce the proposition’s supervisory dimension by extending duties to managing partners, heads of chambers, boards, judges overseeing staff, and lawyers reviewing work produced by associates, clients or tools.

Material variation concerns implementation rather than the core duty. Some sources impose categorical checks for court filings, citations, facts and arguments, while the CCBE and NSW guidance permit task-sensitive assistance and differentiated safeguards for lower-risk work. Some favour disclosure, certification, recordkeeping and contestability; others make disclosure context-dependent and focus on existing professional duties. Product-evaluation research adds that benchmarking particular tools and identifying suitable use cases can inform proportionate deployment, but does not replace verification of the specific legal work. Sources also differ over especially sensitive applications: ordinary drafting and summarisation are generally treated as permissible assistance, whereas judicial decision-making, witness evidence and expert reports attract stronger limits. Two fragmentary or narrowly reliability-focused sources leave their position on the full proposition unclear, but none of the supplied evidence clearly opposes retained human accountability. Because this is a curated selection, this alignment should not be treated as evidence of prevalence across the legal profession or judiciary.

qs.q: Therefore, it is essential that barristers (and all legal practitioners) verify that any sources or authorities cited by such systems actually support the propositions asserted, and ensure that the citations are accurate and extant.
qs.a: Considerations when using ChatGPT and generative artificial intelligence software based on large language models (November 2025 update) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: In those circumstances, practical and effective measures must now be taken by those            within the legal profession with individual leadership responsibilities (such as heads of            chambers and managing partners) and by those with the responsibility for regulating            the provision of legal services.
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources strongly support the proposition that AI assistance leaves professional responsibility with human lawyers and that verification must test substantive legal support rather than merely detect fabricated citations. Across court decisions, judicial practice notes, professional guidance and scholarship, the common reasoning is that existing duties of competence, diligence, candour and supervision continue regardless of how work was produced; lawyers must check accuracy, relevance, currency, completeness, jurisdictional fit and fitness for purpose against authoritative sources. Several sources also reinforce leadership accountability through policies, training and technologically competent supervision, especially as tools become more autonomous. Material variation concerns implementation rather than the core proposition: Singapore expressly scales scrutiny to task risk and practitioner expertise; court-facing guidance imposes especially rigorous checks; California adds stronger controls for agentic systems; Cassata makes supervisors’ understanding of associates’ tools part of effective supervision; and educational sources differ between informed selective use and restricting AI-assisted learning to preserve legal reasoning. Some commentary makes unquantified claims about platform reliability or escalating misuse, but these evidentiary limits do not undermine its support for retained judgment and verification. Because these sources principally corroborate and operationalise the completed proposition—rather than collectively redirecting or materially extending it beyond its existing supervisory and task-sensitive framework—the overall position is Supports.

qs.q: The California Court of Appeal put it well: “To state the obvious, it is a fundamental duty of attorneys to read the legal authorities they cite in appellate briefs or any other court filings to determine that the authorities stand for the propositions for which they are cited.” Noland, 114 Cal.
qs.a: Lnu v. Blanche, No. 24-4790 (9th Cir. June 3, 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The Court finds incompatable the concept that a supervising attorney can properly supervise an associate regarding the proper use of technology provided by the law firm (Artificial Intelligence version of Westlaw), with the concept herein conceded that the supervising attorney does not know how to use it.
